source.title: Subspace Match Probably Does Not Accurately Assess the Similarity of Learned Representations

record.tranche_reason: A hand-constructed network example challenges whether subspace match accurately measures representation similarity: its hidden representations have no subspace match but span isomorphic subspaces.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a hand-constructed example, not a trained-model experiment. The cited findings about independently initialized networks are from other work and are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: A short theoretical note. Its hand-built two-layer example argues that subspace match can report no hidden-layer similarity while the hidden spans are isomorphic. So the similarity verdict depends on the criterion chosen, which bears on V6. It is an argument by construction, not an experiment on trained networks.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that subspace match is likely not a suitable similarity metric for two reasons. Intermediate layers can show no match despite identical outputs, and unmatched layers may still span isomorphic subspaces. They call for better methods.
record.recipe_differences: The paper gives an algebraic, hand-constructed example rather than empirically comparing trained networks with subspace match.
record.method_sensitivity: The example contrasts hidden-layer subspace match with the algebraic isomorphism of the spans; it does not vary the metric's settings or the inputs.
record.problems: The evidence is a single low-dimensional example with hand-chosen weights, not trained models or an empirical comparison across similarity measures. No uncertainty estimates or controls are reported.

untested.parts: No trained networks, no comparison across standard similarity measures (CKA, CCA, kNN), no hyperparameter or input-distribution sweeps.
No networks trained from different seeds. The example only argues that Wang et al.'s low hidden-layer match could be a metric artifact.

record.verdict_notes: Evidence is purely a toy algebraic construction. The note also states there is 'no reason to suspect' different seeds reach different weights, which appears to be a wording slip for the opposite meaning. The verdict should carry low weight. Do not treat it as empirical evidence on trained models.

versions.untested_parts: No scale, capability, architecture, objective, or training comparison.
No vision-language models or paired images and captions.
No networks trained from different initializations; the example uses hand-chosen weights.
The example notes isomorphic hidden subspaces but does not apply or evaluate a mapping between models.
No interpretable features, neurons, or circuits are compared.
Only a hand-constructed example is considered; the study does not sweep similarity measures, settings, or in-distribution versus out-of-distribution inputs.
No convergence plateau or effect of shared training data or objectives is studied.

rows.subject: fully connected feedforward neural network (Example 3.1)
rows.size_stated: two neurons each in the input, hidden, and output layers
rows.operation_detail: Compared hidden-layer neuron activation vectors using subspace match
rows.measure: Subspace match between the hidden-layer activation-vector spans
rows.note: The two hidden-layer activation-vector sets are reported as {[1, 1]ᵀ, [1, 1]ᵀ} and {[1, 0]ᵀ, [1, 0]ᵀ}.
rows.check: Values come from a hand-chosen weight construction, not trained models. The stated activation sets do not cleanly follow from the extracted weights (possible text-extraction garbling), so the numbers rest on the authors' statement.

rows.subject: fully connected feedforward neural network (Example 3.1)
rows.size_stated: two neurons each in the input, hidden, and output layers
rows.operation_detail: Compared the hidden-layer representation subspaces for isomorphism
rows.measure: Whether the hidden-layer activation vectors span isomorphic subspaces
rows.value: Both spans are lines in R² and are isomorphic
rows.note: The isomorphism is stated as an algebraic property; no mapping procedure or loss is evaluated.
rows.check: The isomorphism criterion is trivially satisfied: any two 1-D subspaces of R² are isomorphic. This is a very weak alternative similarity notion, so the contrast with subspace match shows little.

rows.subject: fully connected feedforward neural network (Example 3.1)
rows.size_stated: two neurons each in the input, hidden, and output layers
rows.operation_detail: Compared output-layer neuron activation vectors across the two weight settings
rows.measure: Equality of output-layer neuron activation vectors
rows.value: The activation vectors are identical; each is the zero vector
rows.note: The comparison is between the two hand-chosen network weight settings.
rows.check: Identical output activations are part of the example's set-up (same function, different internals), not a measurement of metric dependence. As extracted, the matrices do not obviously give zero outputs for the tilde network. The reported values cannot be fully verified from the garbled text.

relationships.condition: Hand-constructed 2-2-2 ReLU network with weights chosen by hand, two inputs
relationships.reason: Subspace match reports no hidden-layer match (r1), yet the spans are isomorphic (r2). The similarity verdict depends on the criterion. This is a constructed example only, with a trivially weak alternative criterion.
relationships.display_finding: Subspace matching found no hidden-layer match in the constructed network, although the hidden spans were isomorphic under a weak alternative criterion.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
